newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Next HK justice chief might roll back labour laws.
newsitem.headline: Next HK justice chief might roll back labour laws.

text.p: Hong Kong's future justice chief said on Friday she would review new labour laws that have boosted trade union muscle in the dying days of British rule.
The laws pushed through the Legislative Council in its final pre-handover session on Thursday would be re-examined after the territory's handover, Justice Secretary Elsie Leung said.
Britain gives the colony back to China next Monday night, ending 156 years of colonial rule. The elected chamber will be disbanded and replaced by an unelected interim body.

Leung told reporters the new laws, which considerably beef up trade union powers and grant collective bargaining rights, would be reviewed by the Executive Council, the future cabinet of leader-to-be Tung Chee-hwa.
The laws went through on Thursday despite strong opposition from the business community and officials.

Leung questioned the rationale behind the five private members' bills, which she claimed were a threat to Hong Kong's competitive edge. Hong Kong is currently one of the most competitive economies in the world with very little union power. The bills, which were moved by pro-democracy legislators Lee Cheuk-yan, Lau Chin-shek, and Leung Yiu-chung, significantly strengthen workers' rights.
They allow workers to claim against employers for anti-union discrimination. Workers would also be entitled to a new holiday on May 1 for Labour Day.
A last-minute rush to pass legislation before July 1 has led to too many bills being passed too hurriedly, Leung said.
Government officials claim the bills are not in the long-term interest of employees, and there has been considerable pressure on the post-handover government to scrap them.
Colonial Governor Chris Patten, who leaves next week, said he would sign the bills into law even though they would probably be scrapped after the handover.
Employers' groups hit out at the bills, saying they threatened Hong Kong's competitiveness.
Patten said his constitutional obligations to sign the bills were clear. But he criticised the way they were pushed through.
"I think what happened yesterday had a lot more to do with the decision to dismantle the Legislative Council than with the state of labour relations in Hong Kong," Patten said.

"I think that it's extremely sad that the legislation on labour matters has gone through without the agreement of the Labour Advisory Board...it's a bad precedent...legislation has been pushed through without that consensus."
